title: The Single-Copy Quantum Bandit Is Classical: An Exact Spectral Collapse
abstract: We study multi-armed bandits whose arms supply unknown quantum states and whose mean rewards are defined by a known effect $F$. Each fresh copy may be measured by an arbitrary, adaptively chosen POVM. We prove an exact collapse: the measured relative entropy from an arm state to its confusing reward half-space equals the classical Burnetas-Katehakis functional of $F$'s spectral statistics, and the spectral measurement of $F$ together with an explicit least-favorable state, built from the derivative of the matrix logarithm, forms a saddle point of the underlying measurement game. Consequently, spectral measurement followed by classical KL-UCB is asymptotically instance-optimal among all consistent single-copy policies, in every finite dimension and for every reward effect under the stated nondegeneracy assumptions: adaptive and randomized measurement design cannot improve the leading logarithmic regret coefficient, and neither can storing copies for later single-copy measurement. A self-contained finite-time bound covers general effects and boundary distributions. Any further improvement must come from measurements outside the single-copy class. For consistent policies with arbitrary quantum memory, an amortized relative-entropy argument gives a converse with the Umegaki half-space divergence, and the two per-arm regret floors, $1/K_{\mathrm{inf}}$ and $1/D_{\mathrm{inf}}$, coincide if and only if the arm commutes with $F$. Whether the Umegaki floor is attainable involves a composite quantum Stein problem and a separate reduction to adaptive regret; we pose it as an open problem, with two-copy numerical evidence.
summary: This paper analyzes quantum multi-armed bandits under a single-copy measurement constraint. It proves that the optimal measurement strategy collapses to measuring the reward observable itself, reducing the problem to a classical bandit setting. This establishes that for single-copy learning, quantum memory or adaptive measurement design cannot improve the asymptotic regret bound.
main_problem: Determining the optimal measurement strategy and asymptotic regret bound for sequential learning (multi-armed bandits) when the arms supply unknown quantum states and measurement is limited to a single copy.
main_result: The single-copy quantum bandit problem collapses to a classical bandit problem defined by the spectral statistics of the reward observable, meaning adaptive quantum measurement design offers no asymptotic advantage over measuring the observable directly.
method: The analysis uses quantum information theory tools, including relative entropy, KL divergence, and variational principles, to establish exact equalities between quantum distinguishability measures and classical functionals.
model_or_system: The model involves $K$ arms, each supplying an unknown quantum state $ho_k$ on a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space. Rewards are determined by a known quantum effect $F$, and the learning process is constrained by single-copy measurements.
key_observables: Measured relative entropy, Umegaki relative entropy, Burnetas-Katehakis functional $K_{	ext{inf}}(k)$, and the asymptotic regret coefficient.
important_parameters: The dimension $d$, the number of arms $K$, the reward effect $F$, and the single-copy constraint.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on the 'single-copy' constraint; improvements require measurements outside this class or collective processing.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the degradation of the regret constant as the measurement basis deviates from the optimal spectral measurement ($	heta=0$), showing the single-copy optimum is achieved at $	heta=0$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a hierarchy of bounds for distinguishability, proves the 'Spectral Collapse' theorem equating quantum distinguishability to a classical functional, and then applies this to show that the optimal single-copy policy is classical (SPECTRAL-KL-UCB).
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework showing when quantum advantages vanish in sequential decision-making tasks, suggesting that for certain physical measurements, the problem reduces entirely to classical information theory.
